ican.text: I can distinguish scalar quantities from vectors and represent a vector using directed segments or components.
I can add, subtract and scale vectors geometrically and component by component.
I can find a displacement from two position vectors and interpret the direction of subtraction.
I can calculate magnitude, normalize a nonzero vector and rescale it to a specified magnitude.
I can express a three-dimensional vector in column form or in terms of $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}$.

ku.text: A scalar has magnitude only; examples include distance, speed and mass. A vector has magnitude and direction; displacement and velocity are examples. The zero vector has magnitude zero and no defined direction.

A directed segment $\overrightarrow{AB}$ describes displacement from $A$ to $B$. Equal vectors have equal magnitude and direction even if drawn at different locations. Reversing the direction gives $\overrightarrow{BA}=-\overrightarrow{AB}$.

If $\mathbf{a}=\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\overrightarrow{OB}$ are position vectors, then $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}$. Subtract the starting position from the ending position.

Add vectors head to tail: $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{AC}$. Componentwise, add or subtract corresponding entries. Subtracting $\mathbf{v}$ is the same as adding $-\mathbf{v}$.
For a scalar $k$, multiplying $\mathbf{v}$ by $k$ scales its magnitude by $|k|$. If $k>0$ the direction is unchanged; if $k<0$ it reverses. If $k=0$, the result is the zero vector.

In three dimensions, $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix}v_1\\v_2\\v_3\end{pmatrix}=v_1\mathbf{i}+v_2\mathbf{j}+v_3\mathbf{k}$, where $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}$ are unit vectors along the positive coordinate axes.
The magnitude is $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2}$. It is a nonnegative scalar, not a vector; its units match the units of the components.

For $\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf0$, the unit vector in its direction is $\hat{\mathbf{v}}=\mathbf{v}/|\mathbf{v}|$. To give that direction a specified magnitude $s\geq0$, use $s\hat{\mathbf{v}}$. The zero vector cannot be normalized.

A position vector locates a point relative to the origin; a displacement relates two points. A vector describes a change, so its coordinate components are not automatically the coordinates of the final position.
For motion with constant velocity $\mathbf{v}$, displacement over time $t$ is $t\mathbf{v}$. Include compatible time and distance units when interpreting a resultant.

misc.better: Subtract initial position from final position: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}$.

Magnitude is the scalar $5$, not a vector.

misc.better: Division by $|\mathbf0|=0$ is undefined, and the zero vector has no direction.

misc.weak: Multiplying a vector by $-2$ changes its length to a negative number.
misc.better: Its magnitude doubles and its direction reverses. Magnitude is never negative.

misc.weak: A position vector and any displacement with the same endpoint are the same.
misc.better: A position vector starts at the origin; a displacement depends on both its starting point and ending point.

terms.text: A quantity described by magnitude without direction.
A quantity with magnitude and direction, represented for example by a directed segment or a component column.
The vector from the origin to a point.
The directed change in position from an initial point to a final point.

formula.text: For $\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf0$, the unit vector in its direction is $\mathbf{v}/|\mathbf{v}|$.

worked.prompt: A drone moves in a three-dimensional coordinate system measured in metres. Its initial position is $A=(1,-2,3)$ and a target is at $B=(5,1,-1)$. Let $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ be their position vectors.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ in component form and in terms of $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}$.
parts.a: Subtract start from finish: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}=(5-1,1-(-2),-1-3)=(4,3,-4)$. Thus $\overrightarrow{AB}=4\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}-4\mathbf{k}$ m.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find the distance from $A$ to $B$ and a unit vector in that direction.
parts.a: $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=\sqrt{4^2+3^2+(-4)^2}=\sqrt{41}$ m. Since this is nonzero, the unit direction is $(4,3,-4)/\sqrt{41}$. Its magnitude is $1$.

parts.label: c
parts.q: The drone travels in this direction at constant speed $7$ m/s. Find its velocity vector and the time needed to reach $B$.
parts.a: Scale the unit direction: $\mathbf{v}=\frac7{\sqrt{41}}(4,3,-4)$ m/s. The path length is $\sqrt{41}$ m, so $t=\sqrt{41}/7\approx0.915$ s.

parts.label: d
parts.q: A second displacement is $\mathbf{w}=(-2,1,2)$ m. Find the resultant of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ followed by $\mathbf{w}$ and its magnitude.
parts.a: $\overrightarrow{AB}+\mathbf{w}=(4,3,-4)+(-2,1,2)=(2,4,-2)$ m. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{4+16+4}=2\sqrt6$ m. The final position would be $B+\mathbf{w}=(3,2,1)$.

parts.label: e
parts.q: Find a unit vector opposite to the resultant in part (d).
parts.a: The opposite resultant is $(-2,-4,2)$. Divide by its magnitude $2\sqrt6$ to obtain $(-1,-2,1)/\sqrt6$.

kq.q: Why is the displacement from $A$ to $B$ equal to $\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}$?
kq.model: Travelling from the origin to $A$ and then from $A$ to $B$ gives $\mathbf{a}+\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{b}$. Rearranging gives the result.

kq.q: Why does dividing by magnitude give a unit vector?
kq.model: For nonzero $\mathbf{v}$, scaling by $1/|\mathbf{v}|$ changes its magnitude to $|\mathbf{v}|/|\mathbf{v}|=1$ while preserving its direction.

kq.q: Why can two equal vectors be drawn in different places?
kq.model: A free vector records magnitude and direction, not a unique starting location. Directed segments with the same magnitude and direction represent the same vector.

kq.q: Why can the zero vector not be normalized?
kq.model: Its magnitude is zero, so the normalization formula would divide by zero. It also has no defined direction.
